source.subject: PHYSICS
source.reasoning_observation: Publisher key chooses black. At equal temperature, visible appearance depends on spectral emissivity in the emitting band and conditions, not room-temperature color labels alone; graybody ranking needs assumptions. Preserve key and refer to R01.

target.protected_work: Evaluate an emission ranking from ordinary color labels by distinguishing reflected illumination, spectral emissivity and controlled thermal observations.
target.decisive_route: Two equal-temperature panels have identical visible-band emissivity but different infrared emissivity. Does equal visible brightness establish equal total radiated power? Shortest valid route: No; spectral emissivity elsewhere can differ. Measure calibrated emission over relevant bands.

representation_translation.evidence: Interpret band-limited brightness versus total radiation

reasoning_chain_length.evidence: Construct countermodels and a discriminating measurement

trap_exception_sensitivity.evidence: Visible color at low temperature is not universal hot-surface emissivity

core1a.scientific_construction: A surface can reflect incident light and emit thermal radiation. Its ordinary visible color describes reflected light under illumination; it does not by itself specify spectral emissivity at high temperature. At fixed temperature and comparable geometry, thermal radiance in a given band is emissivity in that band times blackbody radiance. In a supplied graybody model with equal area and environment, larger emissivity means larger net radiative power when hotter than surroundings. A coating can change with temperature, and total infrared power need not rank visible brightness. Therefore the textbook black-surface rule requires a stated spectral or gray approximation. Work with simulated data, not incandescent objects.

worked_anchor.task: At one common temperature, two opaque model surfaces have visible-band emissivities0.8 and0.3. Which has greater emitted radiance in that band?
worked_anchor.reasoning: First, ratio8/3 for equal blackbody radiance in the specified band.

core1a.model_limits: Specified ideal or matched conditions only; supplied quantitative relations do not establish compulsory exam scope.

core1b.task: Two equal-area model surfaces are observed at the same known high temperature in darkness. A is dark in ordinary illumination, B is pale. A report concludes A must emit more visible light and more total radiation. Construct two compatible spectral emissivity scenarios that make the visible ranking differ; specify independent evidence needed for total-power ranking.
core1b.protected_work: Evaluate an emission ranking from ordinary color labels by distinguishing reflected illumination, spectral emissivity and controlled thermal observations.

stages.predict: Predict whether ordinary visible color alone is enough to rank emitted brightness at a different temperature.
stages.attempt: Two equal-area model surfaces are observed at the same known high temperature in darkness. A is dark in ordinary illumination, B is pale. A report concludes A must emit more visible light and more total radiation. Construct two compatible spectral emissivity scenarios that make the visible ranking differ; specify independent evidence needed for total-power ranking.
stages.reconstruct: Ordinary reflected color alone does not bind high-temperature spectral values. Scenario1 visible emissivity A=.8 B=.3; scenario2 A=.3 B=.8 at the operating state; both can be compatible with low-temperature color labels absent stability assumptions. Measure operating-temperature spectral emissivities or calibrated emitted spectrum, control area, T and background; total-power ranking needs full relevant spectrum.
stages.diagnose: Identify where you replaced spectral measurement by a color label or confused radiation with total energy loss.
stages.repair: State the operating band, temperature, emissivity and comparison conditions; provide compatible alternative and a discriminator.
stages.boundary_test: If both are explicitly gray surfaces with stable emissivities .8 and .3, same area and T hotter than surroundings, what follows?

core1b.boundary_response_criterion: A has greater modeled net radiative power; ratio8/3 if surroundings and geometry matched.

core1b.task: A thermal-imaging model reports two panels at equal temperature and geometry. Panel X has higher measured infrared radiance than Y in the sensor band. A student claims X is visibly brighter and necessarily cools faster. Assess both claims and propose a test that separates emissivity from other energy-loss paths.
core1b.protected_work: Evaluate an emission ranking from ordinary color labels by distinguishing reflected illumination, spectral emissivity and controlled thermal observations.

stages.predict: Predict whether higher infrared radiance alone establishes faster cooling.
stages.attempt: A thermal-imaging model reports two panels at equal temperature and geometry. Panel X has higher measured infrared radiance than Y in the sensor band. A student claims X is visibly brighter and necessarily cools faster. Assess both claims and propose a test that separates emissivity from other energy-loss paths.
stages.reconstruct: IR-band ordering alone does not fix visible emissivity or total loss; cooling also depends on thermal capacity, conduction, convection and full spectral emission. Measure visible-band radiance and matched-state steady power or heat capacity plus loss-path controls.
stages.diagnose: Identify where you replaced spectral measurement by a color label or confused radiation with total energy loss.
stages.repair: State the operating band, temperature, emissivity and comparison conditions; provide compatible alternative and a discriminator.
stages.boundary_test: If total net radiative power is independently greater for X but X has twice the thermal capacity, must its temperature initially fall faster?

core1b.boundary_response_criterion: No; compare P_loss/C, including other paths.
